title: Document optimal configuration for FrotzLM
description: Based on benchmark results, document the recommended OmniGen2 configuration for FrotzLM balancing speed and quality. Update CLAUDE.md with findings.
close_reason: Optimal config: --taylorseer --cfg-range-end 0.7 gives 2.2x speedup. TaylorSeer alone is 2x. TeaCache ineffective at default threshold. Resolution scales linearly with pixels.

title: Test spatial composition with multiple objects
description: Generate test images with explicit spatial relationships (e.g., 'object A to the left of object B', 'character blocking doorway', 'item in foreground'). Evaluate how reliably OmniGen2 places objects where specified. Include tests for: foreground/background placement, left/right/center positioning, blocking/occlusion relationships, relative size.
notes:
## Spatial Composition Test Results

Tested OmniGen2's ability to handle explicit spatial relationships. All 5 test categories passed.

### Test Results
- 01_left_right: Lantern left, sword right - PASS
- 02_center: Jade figurine centered on altar - PASS  
- 03_foreground_background: Lantern foreground, archway background - PASS
- 04_blocking: Troll blocking doorway - PASS
- 05_relative_size: Tiny mouse vs giant boots - PASS

### Findings
Strengths: Left/right/center positioning, foreground/background depth, blocking/occlusion, and relative size comparisons all work reliably.

### Conclusion
OmniGen2 handles spatial composition well for text adventure illustration. No additional tools (GLIGEN, ControlNet) appear necessary for basic spatial positioning.

title: Benchmark reduced cfg_range_end
description: Test reducing cfg_range_end from 1.0 to 0.7-0.8. Per paper, this can reduce inference time with negligible quality impact by skipping CFG in later timesteps.
close_reason: cfg-range-end=0.7: ~14% speedup (2:45→2:22). Skips CFG guidance in final 30% of steps. Can combine with TaylorSeer for 2.2x total speedup.

title: Benchmark TeaCache (~30% speedup)
description: Test TeaCache optimization which claims ~30% speedup with minor detail loss. Test different teacache_rel_l1_thresh values (0.05 default, 0.1, 0.15) to find optimal quality/speed tradeoff.
close_reason: TeaCache (thresh=0.05): No speedup observed (2:46 vs 2:45 baseline). Default threshold too conservative. May need higher threshold values or different prompts to see benefit.

title: Benchmark OmniGen2 inference optimizations
description: Systematically benchmark available OmniGen2 speedup options to find the best quality/speed tradeoff for FrotzLM. Options to test: TaylorSeer (~2x), TeaCache (~30%), DPMSolver++ scheduler, reduced cfg_range, flash_attn, and resolution scaling.
close_reason: Completed inference optimization benchmarks. Best config: --taylorseer --cfg-range-end 0.7 (2.2x speedup). flash_attn investigation deferred (frotzlm-lgz remains open).

title: Benchmark DPMSolver++ scheduler
description: Test DPMSolver++ scheduler vs default Euler. DPMSolver++ may converge faster, allowing fewer steps for same quality. Test at 15, 20, 25 steps.
close_reason: Won't do: DPMSolver++/Heun schedulers not compatible with OmniGen2 pipeline (passes custom kwargs like num_tokens that other schedulers don't accept)

title: Benchmark TaylorSeer (~2x speedup)
description: Test TaylorSeer optimization which claims ~2x speedup with negligible quality loss. Compare generation time and output quality against baseline.
close_reason: TaylorSeer: 2.0x speedup (2:45→1:22 for 25 steps at 1024²). Caches intermediate computations and reuses them. Quality appears preserved.

title: Investigate flash_attn compatibility with GB10
description: Flash attention provides ~20-30% speedup but may have compatibility issues with NVIDIA GB10 (sm_121a architecture, CUDA capability 12.1). PyTorch currently only supports up to 12.0. Investigate: (1) if flash_attn can be built for sm_121, (2) if newer flash_attn versions support it, (3) workarounds if any.
close_reason: Investigation complete: Flash-attn on GB10 provides NO benefit. GitHub issue #1969 benchmarks show SDPA (cuDNN 9.13) is actually 2% FASTER than compiled flash-attn on GB10 (481ms vs 489ms). Kernels fall back to generic PTX. OmniGen2 already uses SDPA as fallback - this is optimal for GB10.

title: Evaluate OmniGen2 scene composition and reference-based consistency
description: Systematically test OmniGen2's ability to: (1) reliably compose scenes with multiple objects in specified spatial relationships, (2) use reference images to maintain consistency of characters, objects, and style across generations. This will determine if we need additional tools like GLIGEN/ControlNet or if OmniGen2 alone is sufficient.

title: Test object count accuracy
description: Test how reliably OmniGen2 generates the correct number of objects when specified (e.g., 'three candles', 'two guards'). This is a known weakness of diffusion models.

title: Test small object visibility in complex scenes
description: The jade figurine was missing/hard to see in the Hades scene. Test various approaches: stronger emphasis in prompt, foreground placement language, larger relative size descriptions. Determine if small important objects can be reliably rendered.
notes:
## Small Object Visibility Test Results

All three approaches successfully render small objects prominently:

### Test Results
1. **Strong emphasis** (IMPORTANT, focal point, glows): Object becomes large, glowing, centered
2. **Foreground placement** (bottom third, close to camera): Good size, proper depth composition  
3. **Size + shape description** (palm-sized, 6 inches, seated Buddha): **BEST** - produces detailed, recognizable object

### Recommendations for FrotzLM prompts:
- Use specific size descriptions ("palm-sized", "6 inches tall")
- Describe the object's shape/form ("seated Buddha", "carved jade")
- Add lighting interaction ("catches torchlight", "stands out against")
- Avoid vague "small" - use relative or absolute sizes instead

### Original Issue
The hades scene prompt said "small exquisite jade figurine" which was too vague. Better: "A palm-sized jade figurine carved as a seated figure, its green surface catching the dim light"

### Conclusion
Small objects CAN be reliably rendered when prompts include specific size, shape, and visual contrast descriptions.

title: Create reference image library for key objects
description: Generate and curate reference images for recurring Zork objects: brass lantern, elvish sword, jade figurine, trophy case, mailbox, etc. These will be used to test in-context generation for consistency.

title: Test in-context generation with reference images
description:
Use OmniGen2's native multi-image input to test: (1) style transfer from a reference, (2) object consistency using reference images, (3) combining multiple references (style + object). Measure how faithfully the reference is reproduced.

## Progress (2026-01-07)
- ✅ Single reference test completed: brass lantern in cave scene (test_lantern_scene.png)
- 🔄 Multi-reference test started but interrupted (CPU too slow ~1min/step)
- Reference images created: brass_lantern.png, elvish_sword.png, jade_figurine.png

## Next Steps
1. Run multi-reference test on GPU (lantern + sword in dungeon scene)
2. Test jade figurine visibility in complex scene
3. Evaluate reference adherence quality across all tests
notes:
## In-Context Generation Test Results - COMPLETED

### Tests Performed
1. **Single reference** (brass lantern in cave): ✅ Excellent adherence
2. **Multi-reference** (lantern + sword): ✅ Both objects faithfully reproduced
3. **Reference in complex scene** (jade figurine in Hades): ✅ Much better visibility than without reference

### Key Findings

**Reference Adherence Quality: EXCELLENT**
- Objects closely match reference images in shape, color, and style
- Works with 1-2 references simultaneously
- References help maintain visibility in complex scenes

**Comparison: With vs Without Reference**
- Original hades.png (no ref): Jade figurine barely visible
- With jade reference: Figurine prominently visible, matches ref shape

**Recommendations for FrotzLM**
1. Generate reference images for key Zork objects (lantern, sword, figurine, etc.)
2. Use references when object consistency matters across scenes
3. Reference images help with small object visibility in complex scenes
4. Multi-reference works well for scenes with multiple key objects

### Test Images
- test_references/01_multi_ref_lantern_sword.png
- test_references/02_jade_in_hades.png
- test_lantern_scene.png (existing)

### Conclusion
OmniGen2's in-context generation with reference images works excellently for FrotzLM's use case.

title: Test cross-scene consistency without references
description: Generate the same object/character in multiple different scenes using only text prompts (no reference images). Measure visual drift. This establishes the baseline for how much reference images help.

title: Evaluate if additional tools needed (GLIGEN, ControlNet, etc.)
description: Based on composition and consistency test results, determine if OmniGen2 alone is sufficient or if we need to add: GLIGEN for bounding box layout control, ControlNet for structural guidance, IP-Adapter for stronger reference adherence, StoryDiffusion for cross-scene consistency.

title: Add reference image support to test script
description: Extend test_omnigen2.py to accept --reference-image arguments for in-context generation testing. Support multiple references with prompt syntax like 'the lantern from <img1>'.

title: Add optimization flags to test_omnigen2.py
description: Add CLI flags for: --taylorseer, --teacache (with threshold), --scheduler (euler/dpmsolver++), --cfg-range-end. These will enable benchmarking the various speedup options.
close_reason: Added optimization flags: --taylorseer (~2x speedup), --teacache/--teacache-thresh (~30% speedup), --cfg-range-end. TaylorSeer and TeaCache are mutually exclusive. Scheduler swapping (heun) incompatible with OmniGen2 pipeline.

title: Benchmark resolution scaling
description: Test different output resolutions (512x512, 768x768, 1024x1024) to quantify the time/quality tradeoff. Document which resolution is acceptable for FrotzLM use case.
close_reason: Resolution scaling roughly linear with pixel count: 512² takes 0:48 vs 1024² at 2:45 (3.4x faster for 4x fewer pixels). Use lower resolution for faster iteration.
